setup: Loan to Hazard Corp: commitment USD 120m, of which USD 80m is outstanding today. One-year default probability 1%, loss rate on default 25%. Standard deviation of the default probability 4%, of the loss rate 15%. Unexpected loss on the loan: $UL = EA\sqrt{PD\,\sigma_{LR}^2 + LR^2\,\sigma_{PD}^2}$.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.026m
options.why: Left the square root off: $80 \times 0.000325 = 0.026$. The root is what turns a variance back into a loss amount.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.20m
options.why: Reported the expected loss $80 \times 1\% \times 25\% = 0.20$, not the unexpected loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 8.6m
options.why: Dropped every square, putting $\sigma$ and $LR$ under the root instead of $\sigma^2$ and $LR^2$.

takeaway: UL uses the amount outstanding today, and the root is the last step: UL is a standard-deviation-sized number, far above EL here (1.44 against 0.20).

setup: Loan outstanding USD 80m (commitment 120m). PD 2%, loss rate 25%, standard deviation of PD 14%, of loss rate 15%. Under the root of $UL = EA\sqrt{A + B}$ sit $A = PD\,\sigma_{LR}^2$ and $B = LR^2\,\sigma_{PD}^2$.
ask: Which term under the root is larger?

options.label: $A$, the term with $PD = 2\%$ in it
options.why: Followed the headline PD of 2% (so $A = 0.02 \times 0.0225 = 0.00045$). But $B = 0.0625 \times 0.0196 = 0.001225$ is larger: the large $\sigma_{PD} = 14\%$ matters.

options.label: About equal
options.why: They differ by a factor of about 2.7, not close to equal.

takeaway: Each variance is weighted by the other leg: PD volatility is multiplied by $LR^2$, and loss-rate volatility by PD. A wide $\sigma_{PD}$ can dominate even when PD itself is small.

setup: A sub-portfolio holds 500 loans. Each has a one-year default probability of 1.5%, and defaults are independent. Each loan is a two-state (default / no default) outcome, so the number of defaults is binomial.
ask: The variance of the number of defaults in the sub-portfolio is closest to:

options.why: Gave the variance of a single loan, $0.015 \times 0.985 = 0.0148$, and never multiplied by $n = 500$.
Reported the standard deviation $\sqrt{7.39}$ instead of the variance.
Used $n(1-PD) = 492.5$, the expected number of survivors, in place of $nPD(1-PD)$.

takeaway: Independent variances add: $n\,PD(1-PD)$. With a small PD it sits just below the mean $nPD = 7.5$.

setup: A borrower defaults over one year with probability 2%, modelled as a two-state (binomial) event: it either defaults or it does not.
ask: The variance of this default indicator, compared with the PD of 0.02, is:

options.label: Exactly 0.02
options.why: Treated variance as equal to PD, as if defaults were a rare Poisson-type count. For a two-state event the variance is $PD(1-PD)$.

options.label: Far above 0.02, near 0.14
options.why: Took the standard deviation $\sqrt{0.0196} = 0.14$ for the variance.

takeaway: Two-state variance is $PD(1-PD)$: just under PD when PD is small, and never above 0.25.

setup: Two credit assets with stand-alone unexpected losses $UL_X = \$556{,}417$ and $UL_Y = \$387{,}732$, default correlation 0.4, portfolio UL $\$795{,}317$. The risk contribution of X is $RC_X = UL_X(UL_X + \rho UL_Y)/UL_P$.
ask: Compared with its stand-alone $UL_X$, the risk contribution $RC_X$ is:

options.label: Equal to $UL_X$
options.why: Treated contribution as the stand-alone figure. That holds only at $\rho = 1$; here the ratio is $711{,}510/795{,}317 = 0.89$.

options.label: Above $UL_X$
options.why: Thought positive correlation inflates X's share beyond its own UL. Contributions sum to $UL_P$, which is below $UL_X + UL_Y$.

takeaway: Whenever $\rho < 1$, $RC_i < UL_i$: diversification shows up as a ratio below 1 in front of the stand-alone UL.

setup: Two identical loans to the same industry. Each: exposure USD 50m, stand-alone $UL = \text{USD } 5.5\text{m}$, expected loss USD 0.5m. Default correlation between them is 0.28. The portfolio UL is $\sqrt{UL_1^2 + UL_2^2 + 2\rho UL_1 UL_2}$ and $RC_1 = UL_1(UL_1 + \rho UL_2)/UL_P$.
ask: The risk contribution of each loan is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.5m
options.why: Gave the expected loss, not a risk contribution.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.5m
options.why: Took only the correlation add-on $\rho UL = 0.28 \times 5.5 = 1.54$ and left out the loan's own UL.

options.label: ≈ USD 11m
options.why: Added the two stand-alone ULs ($5.5 + 5.5$): the undiversified portfolio UL, not one loan's share of it.

takeaway: Contributions add up to the portfolio UL. For identical loans each takes exactly half of it, here 4.4 of 8.8.

setup: Two positions with stand-alone ULs of \$16.0m and \$9.4m, default correlation 0.18, portfolio UL about \$20.0m. Contribution: $RC_i = UL_i(UL_i + \rho UL_j)/UL_P$.
ask: Position 1's risk contribution is what share of the portfolio UL?

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Gave the bigger position the smaller share, mixing up which UL goes in front.

options.label: Between 50% and 65%
options.why: Used the stand-alone split $16.0/(16.0 + 9.4) = 63\%$. Correlation tilts contributions further toward the larger position.

takeaway: A contribution sits above the stand-alone share when positive correlation is present: the larger position absorbs more than its stand-alone proportion (71% against 63%).

setup: A large portfolio of near-identical loans with constant pairwise default correlation 0.25. Each loan has a stand-alone UL of CNY 103,400. In the large-portfolio limit, a loan's contribution is $ULC \approx UL\sqrt{\rho}$.
ask: Each loan's contribution to the portfolio UL is:

options.label: A quarter of its stand-alone UL
options.why: Multiplied by $\rho = 0.25$ and forgot the square root.

options.label: The same as its stand-alone UL
options.why: Ignored diversification. With $\rho < 1$ each loan adds less than it would alone.

takeaway: In a big homogeneous pool a loan's contribution is $UL\sqrt{\rho}$. The root makes it larger than $\rho \times UL$.

setup: Two loans: stand-alone ULs of \$235,266 and \$200,000, with default correlation 0.2. If correlation were 0 the portfolio UL would be \$308,788; if it were 1 it would equal the plain sum, \$435,266.

options.label: Below \$308,788
options.why: Treated a positive correlation as if it reduced risk below the uncorrelated case.

options.label: Above \$435,266
options.why: Added the correlation term on top of the plain sum. The plain sum is the ceiling, reached only at $\rho = 1$.

takeaway: Portfolio UL rises from the root-sum-of-squares at $\rho = 0$ to the plain sum at $\rho = 1$; any $0 < \rho < 1$ lands in between.

setup: Credit portfolio of 12 identical assets, each with stand-alone UL JPY 85m, pairwise default correlation 0.3. For identical assets, $UL_P = UL\sqrt{n + \rho(n^2 - n)}$. Economic capital is later $UL_P \times CM$ with $CM = 7.3$.
ask: The portfolio UL is about how many times one asset's UL?

options.label: About 3.5 times
options.why: Used $\sqrt{12}$, which assumes zero correlation.

options.label: 12 times
options.why: Added the 12 stand-alone ULs, which assumes perfect correlation.

takeaway: Zero correlation gives $\sqrt{n}$ times one UL and perfect correlation gives $n$ times; $\rho = 0.3$ puts the multiple between them (7.2 here).

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: Merton model: asset value 120, zero-coupon debt face value 100 due in 1 year, asset volatility 20%, expected asset return $\mu = 8\%$, risk-free rate $r = 3\%$. Distance to default $d_2 = [\ln(A/L) + (m - \sigma^2/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$, where drift $m$ is $\mu$ for the real-world PD and $r$ for the risk-neutral PD.
ask: The real-world PD, compared with the risk-neutral PD, is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Read a higher expected return as more risk. A higher drift lifts $d_2$ and moves the assets further from default.

options.label: The same
options.why: Assumed drift does not matter. It is irrelevant to option pricing, but it does set the real-world PD.

takeaway: Bigger $d_2$ means smaller PD. The real-world drift $\mu$ exceeds $r$ here, so the real-world PD is below the risk-neutral PD.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: A EUR 2,000,000 fixed-rate business loan at 4% with duration 6 years. Rates are expected to rise by 0.75%. The duration approximation is $\Delta L = -L \times D \times \Delta i/(1+i)$. The crude figure $D \times \Delta i$ is $6 \times 0.0075 = 4.5\%$.
ask: The loan's fall in value, as a share of its value, is:

options.label: Exactly 4.5%
options.why: Left out the $1/(1+i)$ divisor and used $D\Delta i$ as the full percentage change.

options.label: Larger than 4.5%
options.why: Multiplied by $1+i$ instead of dividing by it.

takeaway: Modified duration divides by $(1+i)$, so the loss is always a little smaller than $D\Delta i$ when rates are positive.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: A EUR 1,500,000 corporate loan. Spread income (2.5% over cost of funds) is EUR 37,500 and the 1% origination fee is EUR 15,000. Still to deduct: expected loan losses EUR 20,000 and operating costs EUR 15,000, then 30% tax.
ask: The after-tax loan revenue (the RAROC numerator) is closest to:

options.label: EUR 17,500
options.why: Stopped at the pre-tax figure and never applied $(1 - 30\%)$.

options.label: EUR 36,750
options.why: Skipped the expected losses and operating costs: $(37{,}500 + 15{,}000) \times 0.7$.

takeaway: RAROC revenue is (spread + fees - expected loss - operating costs) times $(1 - \text{tax})$: the tax is the last step.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: Two EUR 2,000,000 loans with the same expected losses (0.5% of principal), operating costs (0.4%), tax rate (25%) and capital at risk (EUR 300,000). Loan A: origination fee 1.0%, interest spread 3.0%. Loan B: fee 0.5%, spread 4.0%.
ask: Which loan has the higher RAROC?

options.label: Loan A
options.why: Favoured the larger fee. Fee and spread both count; B's total of 4.5% beats A's 4.0%.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Same costs and capital, but the revenues differ (EUR 46,500 against EUR 54,000).

takeaway: With identical costs, tax and capital, RAROC ranks loans by fee plus spread. Here that sum is 4.5% against 4.0%.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: A USD 750,000 loan with duration 2.85 and an interest rate of 9.5%. Rates are expected to rise by 1.25%. Capital at risk is the duration-based fall in value, $L \times D \times \Delta i/(1+i)$.

options.label: Below USD 20,000
options.why: Left out the duration: $750{,}000 \times 0.0125/1.095 \approx 8{,}560$.

takeaway: The $1/(1+i)$ divisor shaves about 9% off the capital figure, which is enough to move this one below USD 25,000 and lift RAROC to about 8.1%.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: A EUR 2,000,000 loan (EAD = loan value, LGD 45%). Default rates are assumed normal with standard deviation 2%, and the bank uses the 99.5% confidence level, $\alpha = 2.6\sigma$. Capital at risk is the unexpected loss $\alpha \times LGD \times EAD$.
ask: Capital at risk is closest to:

options.label: EUR 18,000
options.why: Used $\sigma = 2\%$ itself instead of $\alpha = 2.6\sigma = 5.2\%$.

options.label: EUR 104,000
options.why: Left out the 45% LGD: $5.2\% \times 2{,}000{,}000$.

takeaway: Capital at risk takes the confidence multiple on the default rate, then scales by loss given default and exposure: $\alpha \times LGD \times EAD$.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: Loan with EAD USD 10,000,000 and LGD 40%. Spread 0.60%, fees 0.25%, expected loan losses 0.20%, operating costs 0.15%, tax 25%. Capital at risk is the unexpected loss $\alpha \times LGD \times EAD$ with $\alpha = 5\%$. RAROC is after-tax revenue divided by capital at risk.
ask: The loan's RAROC is closest to:

options.why: Divided the after-tax revenue ($0.375\%$ of the loan) by the loan amount rather than by capital at risk.
Left the LGD out of capital at risk ($0.05 \times 10{,}000{,}000 = 500{,}000$).
Read $\alpha = 5\%$ as $0.5\%$, a decimal-place slip that shrinks capital tenfold.

takeaway: RAROC divides a revenue of a few tenths of a percent of the loan by capital of a few percent: expect a double-digit result, not a fraction of a percent.
